item.title: Talking Zen 6 with Mike Clark at AMD In-Depth
item.description:
Hello you fine Internet folks,I sat down with AMD’s Mike Clark to talk about Zen 6, the evolution from Zen 5 and what some of the differences are between Zen 6 and Zen 6c and what drove some of those changes.

Hope y’all enjoy!

The transcript below has been edited for readability and conciseness.

George Cozma: Hello, you fine Internet folks. We’re here at AMD In-Depth, where we’re talking about Venice. With me, I have a returning guest, Mike Clark. Would you like to tell the audience who you are?

Mike Clark: Hi, I’m Mike Clark, the original architect of Zen. Some people refer to me as “Zen Daddy.” I’ve been working on cores here at AMD for 33 years, and we’ve got another great one coming, so I’m very proud of the design team I get to represent here today.

George Cozma: I’ve had some hands-on time with Zen 6c. Let’s talk about the change that’s happened with Zen 6 and Zen 6c, what I refer to in my piece as the Zen 6 family. Why is it different from previous generations?

Mike Clark: Right. Starting with Zen 4, we’ve been going through this evolution of having two core families. Before, we were really just using the denser technology as an area play. In this generation, having learned a lot, as we were filling out that denser version of the core, we wanted to leverage it to add some extra IPC within the core. So if you look more in-depth at what we have, what used to be our classic design, we now think of as our high-frequency design. And our dense technology is now our top-of-the-line, no-questions-asked performance core, because we’ve also enabled the full L3 in that implementation, at 4MB per core. So we have 32 of those cores, 128MB of L3, and the highest IPC you can get in that core.

George Cozma: Awesome. So far, one thing I’ve noticed is that the vector scheduler is a bit bigger on Zen 6c. What was the reasoning for increasing that on Zen 6c?

Mike Clark: Well, that wasn’t the only thing we increased. One principle we follow is that we don’t want to create a delta between the two architectures that software has to be optimized for. We want them to have the same fit and feel, so the same optimizations apply to both. But because of its reduced frequency target, Zen 6c can have a little more capacity in the queues, since it doesn’t have to reach the maximum frequency the high-frequency core has to hit. The floating-point scheduler is just one example. There are other queues throughout the core that are larger in Zen 6c, to pull out a little more IPC and get a little more leverage in that SMT environment as well.

George Cozma: Interesting. Both Zen 6 and Zen 6c build on the design you had in Zen 5, and one of the interesting things with Zen 5 was the dual decode setup. Has the front end changed much to let a single thread make better use of both decode clusters?

Mike Clark: Yes. As you said, Zen 5 was a new foundation, with the ability to fetch two basic blocks and get them down the line. But it gets quite complicated with one thread running larger-footprint workloads, where some of it might be hitting the I-cache and some of it might be hitting the op cache, and you’re trying to get everything synced up. So we spent a lot of time optimizing that and making it more efficient from both a delivery and a power perspective: less power wasted, and more efficient delivery from that new front end.

George Cozma: Awesome. Going down into the execution engine, I also noticed that the number of integer multiply units has gone down from three to two. Could you talk a bit about what drove that choice?

Mike Clark: It really came out of the Zen 5 design, where we had a more unified scheduler. To make a scheduler simpler, you want the units it schedules into to be very uniform, and the way we had set up those schedulers, adding a third multiplier to the group it was scheduling into was easy and didn’t add complication. In Zen 6, we realized that to really scale out the architecture, we needed to go back to more distributed schedulers, which now schedule into the ALUs. We hadn’t seen much uptick from that extra multiplier on Zen 5, so to optimize the area and the schedulers, we went back to two multipliers.

George Cozma: Speaking of integer multiply, on the vector side you’ve added two more VNNI units. What was the impetus for adding them, and at what point in the design did you add them?

Mike Clark: As I said in the talk, these are long design programs. We weren’t designing Zen 6 to be an agentic core. When we started, no one was really even using that term. But Zen 5 was a whole new foundation for AI workloads, and we’ve always believed the core has a place in AI: orchestration, data type manipulation, smaller models. So we were always focused on making the core good at AI. It’s not going to beat a GPU, and that’s not the point. We realized we probably should have some more VNNI, given where we were seeing inference go, and the team rallied around that. It was kind of late, since these are long-lead projects and the floor plan was set, but the team rallied, we were able to squeeze a couple more VNNI pipes in there, and it was a big success.

George Cozma: Again on the vector side, one of the oddities of Zen 5 was that although the wires were all there, the load unit could only do two vector loads at a time. What changed within the Zen 6 core to allow four vector loads, assuming they’re either 128 or 256 bits?

Mike Clark: We can do the 256-bit loads. Since we were able to do two 512-bit loads, we already had 1,024 wires headed over there. Obviously, using them piecemeal versus as one contiguous set complicates the design. I think it’s something we always wanted to do on Zen 5, but with all the change and getting it working, we left that for the Zen 6 team, and they were awesome. We’re all really one team at AMD anyway, and sometimes things intersect at different points in the roadmap. This was the time to do it.

George Cozma: Speaking of bandwidth into the caches, the L2 in Zen 5 had some oddities where it couldn’t always hit 64 bytes per cycle on reads. What changed in Zen 6 to allow that? Because I’ve been able to measure it, and it does hit that.

Mike Clark: Honestly, sometimes you just don’t see some of these things. A lot of it was that we would be over-prefetching, and prefetches that hit in the L2 would be robbing L2 bandwidth. So we made sure we could sustain those prefetches alongside demand requests, reduce the conflicts, and deliver the full 64 bytes per cycle that we want.

George Cozma: Awesome. Circling all the way back to the front: the all-important branch predictor. There seems to have been a reduction in branch misprediction latency, so when you miss a branch, the number of cycles it takes to recover has gone down. What I also noticed, which is really neat, is that there wasn’t any reduction in accuracy. So how did you pull off not only a faster branch predictor, but one that’s even slightly more accurate than Zen 5’s already very accurate predictor?

Mike Clark: The branch prediction team, as you know, is very algorithmic. There’s lots of design space and lots of exploration, and AI has even been getting involved in helping us figure out how to optimize it. It’s a great optimization problem: the number of TAGE tables, how much information they hold, accuracy. So we set out to make a more efficient one. That was an area where we didn’t really want to grow; we thought we could be more efficient in the way we lay out the tables for prediction. And we’re always focused on our pipeline length. No matter how good a branch predictor you build, there are always hard-to-predict branches, and you’re always going to mispredict. So each generation, we’re monomaniacally focused on getting going again as fast as we can when we’re wrong. There are lots of unique tricks we pull to get that redirect back into the front end and get it flowing as fast as possible. And you’ve observed it, which is great.

George Cozma: Yeah. I haven’t had time on Zen 6 yet, but I have had time on Zen 6c, and in SPECint 2026 it matches your fastest Zen 5 server CPU. That’s very impressive, especially considering the clock deficit. Wrapping this all up and moving outside the core into the L3, there are obviously topology differences between the 12-core and 32-core CCDs. How much were you able to mitigate those differences inside the core, building up structures to tolerate latency, to compensate for the slightly increased L3 latency?

Mike Clark: As I always talk about, the design has to be balanced. As we grow the capacity of a structure, the new technology helps it shrink, so the physical distance doesn’t grow linearly, but unfortunately the distance does grow. Inside the L3, there are a lot of tricks I can’t talk about...

George Cozma: The secret sauce!

Mike Clark: [In order to] maintain bandwidth within the L3 mesh so we can keep delivering to the cores. And in the cores, we do grow the queues to handle those higher latencies.

George Cozma: Awesome. My penultimate question: Verano is adding LPDDR5X to the EPYC ecosystem. Were there any design considerations between LPDDR5X and DDR5 that you had to think about when designing the core?

Mike Clark: At the CCX level, we focus a lot on bandwidth per core. I think Mahesh talked a lot about the SDP ports, with 32-byte reads per port, so we try to make sure we have enough bandwidth between the CCD and the IOD. But we were already well provisioned for bandwidth with MRDIMMs, so that construction, the winglets and choosing a different memory technology, didn’t really have a major impact on how we built the core.

George Cozma: Awesome. Usually this is where I’d ask what your favorite type of cheese is, but since we already know that: have you tried any new cheeses lately?

Mike Clark: I have. My new favorite is Cotija cheese.

George Cozma: Oh!

Mike Clark: I’ve been eating a lot of tacos.

George Cozma: You’ve got to love Cotija on tacos. It’s absolutely amazing. Well, thank you so much for sitting down with me. If you like videos like this, hit like and subscribe; it does help with the algorithm. There are PayPal and Patreon links in the description, as well as a transcript of this on the Chips and Cheese website. Thank you so much.

Mike Clark: Thanks for having me, George. I always look forward to coming and talking with you about what this awesome AMD CPU design team has created, and you always have so many good questions. I wish I could answer more, since we do have to protect our secret sauce, but I really enjoy helping you understand some of our thought processes, the challenges we face, and how we’ve been able to overcome them.

George Cozma: Well, it’s always fun to sit down with you and talk, not just about what you’re doing, but also what the team is doing and what you’re looking forward to in the future. So thank you so much.

Mike Clark: Thank you.

George Cozma: I’ll see you in the next one. Have a good one, folks!

What would your AI red lines be?

Decide now what would make you act on AI, and what you'd do. Then share it.

Writing a red line down is a start. These steps make it more likely you'll keep it. Do each one, or skip it, and the next one opens.

From a 2016 review of 138 trials with 19,951 people (Harkin and others, Psychological Bulletin). In each trial, some people were prompted to keep track of a goal and others weren't. On average, the people who were prompted did better at reaching it.

Keeping track helped more when other people could see it (0.55) or when it was reported to someone (0.47) than when it stayed private (0.19). It helped more when people kept a written record (0.43) than when they didn't (0.29).

Joseph Rotblat was a Polish physicist working in Liverpool when the war began. In 1944 he went to Los Alamos with the British team on the Manhattan Project. He had one reason for being there: the fear that Nazi Germany would build an atomic bomb first.

item.title: Fitting Four 32 GB Resizable Bars Behind a PCIe Switch on Linux
item.description:
Fitting Four 32 GB Resizable BARs Behind a PCIe Switch on Linux

My PCIe switch is a Broadcom PEX88096 in the board’s one x16 slot, with four AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700s and the two RTX 3090s from my PCIe splitter post behind it, and the build post has the whole box.

The switch gives each card eight lanes and lets the cards copy to each other without going through the CPU. AMD’s ROCm calls that peer-to-peer (P2P), and it only turns it on when each card’s whole 32 GB is mapped. On Linux, that means a 32 GB Resizable BAR on every card. A base address register, or BAR, maps a range of the CPU’s address space onto a device’s memory. Resizable BAR is the BIOS option that lets a card’s BAR be the full 32 GB instead of the default 256 MB.

A few people asked for the module after the build post, so it’s on GitHub as gpu-rebar-layout. It leans on kernel internals that could change in any release, so read the README before you load it. A patch series on the mailing list fixes the sizing bug, but this board will still need the module’s resize and rescan after it lands, with its padding turned off (pad=0).

Why the BIOS can’t map six 32 GB BARs 🔗

With the 3090s added, the board stopped at the white VGA light on its POST LEDs, because every 32 GB BAR takes up 64 GB of the BIOS’s address space. The address space post has the math.

Linux 7.0’s bridge window sizing bug: can’t assign; no space 🔗

This board’s BIOS has no per-card Resizable BAR setting. Linux can give large BARs to some cards and leave others small, as long as it does it before any GPU driver loads. With all six cards in and Resizable BAR off, I wanted Linux to do the allocation. The plan was to set each R9700’s BAR size register to 32 GB, remove the CPU port the switch hangs off, and rescan, so the kernel lays out the whole switch again from the new sizes.

Each R9700’s 32 GB BAR is followed by a doorbell BAR, for registers the driver writes to tell the card there’s new work. With Resizable BAR on, the BIOS makes it 256 MB. Linux leaves it at 2 MB.

The kernel gave the switch a window of about 128.6 GB. With the doorbell placed after each BAR, the way Linux 7.0 lays them out, the four windows span 224 GB (three 64 GB slots plus the last card’s 32 GB and its doorbell). Two R9700s got their BARs, and the rest of the switch got nothing.

pci 0000:1b:00.0: bridge window [mem size 0x800200000 64bit pref]: can't assign; no space

That was on 7.0.6. The unpatched v7.4-rc1 kernel placed three of the four in the control run that the Linux kernel patch-testing post (coming soon) covers.

0x800200000 is 32 GB plus 2 MB, one card’s window. The kernel had sized the switch’s window as the plain sum of its children: four of those plus the two 3090s’ 288 MB windows.

The function is pbus_size_mem() in drivers/pci/setup-bus.c. For each child of a bridge it adds the child’s size, or its alignment if that’s bigger, to the total.

r_size = resource_size(r); size += max(r_size, align);

That leaves no gap when every child’s size is a multiple of its alignment, which is true for ordinary BARs because they’re powers of two. A GPU’s window here is 32 GB plus 2 MB with a 32 GB alignment, so the sum leaves out the gap of almost 32 GB between one card’s doorbell and the next card’s start.

It’s a known regression. Nikolas Britton reported it on linux-pci in September, and the thread’s title describes my problem almost word for word.

Ilpo Järvinen, who maintains this code, has a fix in a 14-patch series of resource placement fixes, at v5 as of November 6 and not merged yet. I tested it and sent a Tested-by to the linux-pci mailing list. With it, all four R9700s get their 32 GB.

Even with the fix, this board still needs something to set the BAR sizes and rescan before the GPU drivers load, because amdgpu’s resize at load time can’t grow a window that other cards already sit in.

A kernel module that pads the BARs 🔗

The kernel already knows how to raise a BAR’s alignment without changing its size, but naming a device in the pci=resource_alignment= boot option uses the resizing mode instead. Asking for 32 GB alignment on an R9700 would also grow its small BARs, including the 512 KB register BAR, which can’t be aligned to 32 GB below 4 GB.

The workaround is an out-of-tree module that runs from the initramfs, the tiny early-boot filesystem the kernel starts from, before any GPU driver loads. For each matching card it sets the BAR size register, then it removes the root port above the switch and rescans.

Between the scan and the address assignment it walks every bus segment under the switch. It raises each smaller 64-bit prefetchable BAR’s alignment to the size of the largest 64-bit prefetchable BAR on that segment, and does the same for the other memory BARs as a separate group. Each R9700 window becomes exactly 64 GB and each 3090 window exactly 512 MB. Once every window is a multiple of its alignment, the kernel’s allocator does the rest.

After a reboot the R9700s sat at 160, 224, 288, and 352 GB, the 3090s just above them, and amdgpu reported the whole card.

amdgpu 0000:14:00.0: [drm] Detected VRAM RAM=32624M, BAR=32768M

With the ACS redirect setting the box already had (pci=disable_acs_redir= on the R9700 switch ports), P2P between the R9700s ran at 14.0 GB/s for every pair, which is what an eight-lane gen4 link delivers in practice, and all four copying in a ring at once moved 54.7 GB/s.

If your GPUs won’t all get their BARs 🔗 Search the linux-pci mailing list for your can't assign error first. Someone may have already reported it, or even fixed it. Resize the BARs and rescan before the GPU drivers load, which means doing it from the initramfs. Don’t remove or rescan a GPU that already has its driver loaded. That locked up my box. If one card gets its BARs and the next one doesn’t, look at the small BARs next to the big ones. Check the cards again a few minutes after boot, in case they go to sleep and don’t wake back up.

I had help with this one. Claude wrote the module with me, ran the commands and tests on the box over SSH, and helped me draft this post. I did the physical work, read all the words, checked the numbers, and rewrote anything that sounded like a chatbot, so the mistakes are mine.

item.title: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices
item.description:
Every device around you is more capable than it looks. TV boxes, old phones, single-board computers and routers all ship with CPUs, RAM and flash that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing is about unlocking that capability: finding the biggest language model each device can really run, then pushing it further with custom kernels, smarter memory use and weight streaming. Every claim is measured on the hardware itself.

Device #1 is a Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen): Amlogic S7D, 4× Cortex-A55 @ 2.5 GHz, 1.9 GB of RAM (about 1 GB usable), eMMC flash, Android 14, no root. On it, this repo runs models from 260 K to 16 B parameters:

Qwen3.5-0.8B: 16.8 tok/s (2.2× the stock 7.5; measured in the evening of 11-05, see §17). Qwen3.5-2B: 7.7 tok/s in real chat. The box's speed drifts by ~10 % over a day, so every step is measured back to back: §16 gave +11 %, §17 another +7 %. An 8B mixture-of-experts model (Moon-Beam-8B-A1B): 7.2 tok/s in real chat, its experts paged from flash on demand and prefetched one layer ahead (§19). A dense 1-bit 8B model (Bonsai-8B): 5.2 tok/s in real chat, up from 1.2: fully resident in a "headless" mode plus a lookup-table kernel (§19). A 16B mixture-of-experts model (Ling-mini-2.0): 5.1 tok/s in real chat, coherent over 600-word answers, the same expert pager applied unchanged (§20). Twice Moon-Beam's size, but not better per byte: bigger only helps on this box when the model is also better. A dense 9B model: 0.27 tok/s, streaming most of its weights from flash.

Device #2 is a first-generation iPad Air (2013): Apple A7, 2 cores, NEON without dotprod, 1 GB of RAM, iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken, CPU only. A 13-year-old tablet runs a 1.7B-parameter model at 24-26 tok/s (18-22 in long chats), a 4B one at about 10 tok/s, an 8B mixture of experts at about 3.5 tok/s (5 with half its experts, at a quality cost), and a 16B one at 2.6-4.5 tok/s, with their experts paged from flash, from a chat page in its own Safari. See Results on device #2.

Every step is written up experiment by experiment in EXPERIMENT.md (E1-E160).

Physics of the box: one process can hold ~0.96 GB before Android starts killing things (~1.15 GB in headless mode, with the launchers and Google services force-stopped), and flash reads top out at 278 MB/s, with a lone ~1 MB random read costing ~6 ms. That, not the CPU, is what limits everything above 2B, and why a mixture-of-experts model, which touches ~1 B of its 8 B weights per token, is the way past it.

How Bonsai-1.7B got from 2.75 to about 25 tok/s (same model file throughout):

Step tok/s What changed Stock llama.cpp, 2 threads 2.75 emulates dotprod with widening multiplies Multiplication-free NEON kernel 3.45 weights are ±1, so no multiply is needed; output identical Lookup-table kernel from device #1, ported to base NEON about 11 its dotprod requirement turned out to be only an assumption The output head on that kernel 18-22 151,669 rows isn't a multiple of 32, so the tied head had never reached it: 45 of 72 ms per token Row-order attention with pruning, and a sampler that doesn't sort the vocabulary 23.7-25.8 the KV cache stores all heads of a row side by side, so one head at a time missed the cache constantly

In long chats (400-token answers), the three turns went from 15.4 / 7.6 / 8.2 to 21.8 / 17.9 / 18.4 tok/s through the attention work alone. The pruning threshold that holds long chats above 17 costs +0.42 % perplexity at 1,024 tokens of context, near the ±0.3 % noise floor; GGML_FA_EPS=0.0001 trades that back for about 15 tok/s.

An 8B model, through an expert pager. iOS 12 caps a process at about 1.7 GB of mapped address space (1.3 GB for the web server's user), so Moon-Beam-8B's 2.6 GB file can't even be mapped, and keeping fewer experts to make it fit more than doubles its perplexity (§21.7). Dense Bonsai-8B runs at 0.08 tok/s from flash. So the model file is rewritten with its experts last, only the 474 MB before them is mapped, and each layer keeps 14 experts in RAM, reading the others from flash with pread when the router picks them. Results match the unpaged model exactly. A small routing bias toward experts already in RAM (+0.3 % perplexity, inside the noise) brought it to 2.4-2.8 tok/s in about 600 MB (§21.8). Round 2 (§21.9) queues flash reads by when they're needed, prefetches the next layer's likely experts, and runs the experts through a lookup-table kernel for Q2_K: 3.4 tok/s, 40× the dense 8B, at +0.7 % perplexity on the full eval text. The flash is still the limit: each token reads about 53 MB at 266 MB/s. Wiring weights in RAM kernel-panicked the iPad, like a pool of 16 did before. Round 3 (§21.10) evicts by decayed use frequency instead of recency, for 3.5 tok/s at no quality cost. 5 tok/s takes 4 experts per token instead of 8 (+27 % perplexity); choosing the count per token adaptively turned out no better than a fixed count. A 16B model (§21.11): Ling-mini-2.0, 16.3B parameters with 256 small experts per layer, runs through the same pager at 2.6 tok/s with unchanged routing, 3.3 at +2.6 % perplexity and 4.5 with a strong cache bias, in under 580 MB. Its 5.5 GB file was assembled from two published quantizations over HTTP range requests and streamed straight to the iPad, since the Mac had no room for it. It is twice Moon-Beam's size at the same speed, but not a better model (+3 % perplexity).

Limits worth knowing. Bonsai is a 1-bit model and still gets facts wrong (in one test it called Mercury the closest planet to Earth). About 700 MB is the practical memory ceiling: 1-bit weights don't compress, so iOS starts killing processes past it, which is why the 4B needs a 512-token context. The jailbreak doesn't survive a reboot. The fast output head adds 2-3 s to the first prompt after each launch.

Kernels for Cortex-A55 (ARMv8.2 dotprod, no i8mm), as a patch on llama.cpp v0.8.0, each with an exactness test against a scalar reference:

Merging adjacent scales costs +0.18 % perplexity Ternary-Bonsai-4B 3.2 → 4.3 tok/s in chat, prompt 7.0 → 9.6 E76, E77 1-bit lookup-table kernel (Four-Russians / T-MAC style): 32 rows per group, one 16-entry table per 4 activations built straight from the float activations, ~8 NEON ops + 2 loads per 128 multiply-adds vs 16 + 4 Bonsai-8B 3.77 → 5.1-5.4 tok/s (with E82, E88) E81 Q8_0 attention with a threshold: all K dots first with sdot, so the softmax maximum is known up front, then expf and V work skipped for rows below max + ln(1e-4) a 1,000-token answer no longer halves the speed (2.50 → ~4 tok/s at the end) E86 Guided matmul scheduling: each thread grabs remaining / (2 × threads) rows, so a slow or preempted thread leaves a short tail instead of ~28 ms per token of idle cores; single-row element-wise ops split by columns (ggml left them all on thread 0) 2B 6.26 → 6.54 tok/s; 0.8B +1.4 % E63, E64

Memory tricks:

Pruned LM head: keep only the ~49-66 K most useful vocabulary rows, chosen by token frequency on English, code and 7 other languages. The other logits are scattered to −inf. Saves 0.2-0.5 GB and misses ~1 % of English tokens. Repack cache on flash (GGML_REPACK_CACHE): repacked weights are written to a file once and mapped afterwards. Models load in seconds.

Headless mode (tools/tv-llm-mode.sh on|off): a small foreground activity, then the launchers, Google services and other heavy apps are force-stopped, and svc power stayon keeps the animated screensaver (17 % of a core) away. Nothing persistent except stay-awake, which off restores. MemAvailable ~1000 → ~1300 MB. A fork-free guard (tools/tv-watch.c) replaced a shell loop that started ~25 processes a second and cost 10 % of the speed.

Expert pager for mixture-of-experts models (ggml-cpu/moe-pager-tv.inc):

Experts live on flash: each expert tensor is overlaid with empty anonymous memory, and right after a layer's routing the missing experts are read with parallel O_DIRECT straight into their own addresses; a per-layer LRU pool (43 of 128 experts) keeps the rest. Kernels see an ordinary tensor. The GGUF's own expert bytes are hole-punched once the repack cache holds them, so the model costs one copy of its weights on flash. Cache-aware routing (GGML_MOE_BIAS): a small bonus for experts already in RAM cuts misses from 13 % to ~2 % for a measured quality cost (arXiv 2412.00099 has the idea on other models). Fewer experts per token (LLAMA_MOE_USED=6) is the other dial. Warm start from a list of each layer's most used experts, and pre-gated prefetch: layer L+2's router applied to layer L's hidden state, predicting what the router will actually pick (sigmoid, the model's own selection bias and the cache bonus), loads ~60 % of misses before they are needed. Why answers looped, and the fix: 2-bit experts break long-form coherence after ~250-300 words, and routing bias amplifies it. DRY sampling only hides it (the model paraphrases its loop); a repeat penalty of 1.15 over 256 tokens brings degenerate long answers from 12/13 to 1/13 on the TV (E99, E100).

Weight streaming for models bigger than RAM (ggml-cpu/stream-tv.inc):

What stays in RAM: a chosen part of the weights stays resident. The rest lives in "stream zones". Prefetch: a hook on every matmul records the order the weights are used. Reader threads then fetch zone weights ahead of time with parallel 8 MB O_DIRECT reads straight into the weights' own addresses, at the flash's full 278 MB/s. Correctness: every compute thread waits until its weight is completely loaded, so a wrong prediction costs time, never correctness. Drop-behind: each zone weight is freed right after use. Verify mode: GGML_STREAM_VERIFY=1 compares every streamed tensor with the file. It found two silent-corruption bugs, which are fixed and documented in E48 and E50. Speculative decoding: with the model's own MTP head, verifying 2 tokens costs about one pass over the weights when the pass is flash-bound, so it pays off (+69 %). On the in-RAM 2B it lost (E31).

Profiling (env switches in the patch): GGML_OPPROF=1 per-op table, GGML_OPPROF=2 a node-by-node, per-thread trace of one graph (tools/optrace.py), LLAMA_UBATCH_PROF / GGML_CPU_PROF phase timings. They showed where a small model's time really goes (E57): ~71 % Q4_K matmuls, and only ~2 ms per token of barriers and scheduling.

Tooling:

Streaming GGUF rewriter: adds a pruned head, extra tensors and metadata in one sequential pass, so Hugging Face → Mac → TV pipelines never store the model on the Mac. MTP fetcher: range-reads only the MTP tensors from safetensors. Memory guard: wraps every heavy run on the TV. Benchmark and perplexity harnesses, a model screener that streams any Hugging Face GGUF to the TV and scores it (tools/screen-small.sh), and a live token-stream web UI.

You need: the TV box (or another ARMv8.2 Android device) with network ADB, adb, zig (for static aarch64 musl builds), cmake + ninja, python3, and uv (for numpy).

On this box the 2B at 4 bits beats every bigger model at 1-2 bits. Post-training quantization below ~2.5 bits breaks normal models (E22, E23, E35). Models trained for 1-bit or ternary hold up, but at 4-8 B they don't fit without streaming. Past RAM, flash bandwidth sets the speed. The kernel's LRU is the worst possible policy for a cyclic scan bigger than the cache: it re-reads everything every token. Keep a fixed resident set and stream the rest yourself. Batching is free when you are flash-bound. Prompts and speculative verification cost about one weight pass, whatever their size. Measure, then verify. Two streaming bugs gave plausible speeds and wrong numbers; only comparing tensors with the file, and perplexity with a Mac reference, caught them. Small models are mostly vocabulary. Qwen3.5-0.8B's 248K-row head is a third of its weights; pruning it to 65K rows plus all-Q4_K took it from 7.5 to 12.1 tok/s (E55). Small models also lose more to 4 bits (+7 % perplexity vs +2.3 % for the 2B). Simulate before you write a kernel. Activation sparsity (E58) and a low-rank head (E60) both looked promising on paper; a quality simulation on the Mac killed each in under an hour. On an in-order core, count NEON ops as well as bytes. Tighter packing saved 20 % of the bytes and cost 2.5× the ops; undoing it made the 4B 33 % faster in chat (E76, E77). The 4-bit kernel is the opposite case, limited by RAM (E27), so the trick does not help the 2B or 0.8B. Check that every big matrix reaches the fast kernel. The 2B's head (65,668 rows, ~10 % of each token's weights) silently ran on the generic kernel for weeks because ggml only repacks row counts divisible by 8; four extra rows gave +5.8 % (E71, E72). The load log's repack buffer size gives it away. Most of the RAM was Android's, not the model's. Force-stopping the launchers and Google services for the duration (nothing persistent) let Bonsai-8B sit fully in RAM: 1.2 → 3.6 tok/s before any kernel work (E80). An animated screensaver and a guard that forked 25 times a second each cost another 10-15 % (E82, E88). For a mixture-of-experts model the flash is a cache miss, not a stream. A ~6 ms miss per expert means the pool hit rate decides the speed; routing toward cached experts and prefetching what the next router will pick turned 4.4 into 7.2 tok/s. Perplexity can't see loops. It scores one token at a time on clean text; the 2-bit model scored fine and still fell into loops in 12 of 13 long answers. Score long free-running generations too (tools/loop_stats.py), and compare models with different tokenizers in bits per byte, never in perplexity. Past 9B, count resident bytes, not parameters. The ceiling for a mixture-of-experts model here is the non-expert weights that must stay in RAM plus a useful expert pool. Ling-mini-2.0 (16B) keeps 279 MB resident and runs at 5 tok/s; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B would need ~870 MB before caching a single expert (§20). Guard the box. After two early kernel panics, every heavy run goes through a wrapper that kills it below 180 MB of free memory.

MIT. The llama.cpp patch is a derivative of llama.cpp (MIT). Model weights keep their own licenses, and the evaluation texts are Wikipedia excerpts (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Built on llama.cpp and llama2.c. Models from Qwen, unsloth (GGUFs and importance matrices), PrismML (Bonsai), Google (Gemma) and stories260K. The evaluation texts are excerpts from Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). The 🤏 logo is the pinching-hand emoji from Google's Noto Emoji (Apache 2.0).

item.title: ExcalidrawZ: Local Native Excalidraw on macOS/iOS
item.description:
Excalidraw is an excellent drawing tool. ExcalidrawZ keeps the familiar Excalidraw canvas, then adds native file management, iCloud sync, history, export, AI assistance, MCP integration, and Apple-platform interaction details around it.

Non-App Store version

Download the latest .dmg from Releases. Open the .dmg and drag ExcalidrawZ into Applications.

ExcalidrawZ manages drawings as real app documents instead of loose browser downloads.

Organize drawings with groups and custom file sorting. Work with ExcalidrawZ library files, local folders, and temporary external files. Open and edit .excalidraw, .excalidraw.png, and .excalidraw.svg files directly. Sync app-managed files across macOS, iPadOS, and iOS with iCloud. Keep file history checkpoints so important changes can be reviewed and restored.

ExcalidrawZ records checkpoints for app-managed drawings, so you can review earlier versions and restore important work when needed.

The canvas remains compatible with Excalidraw while the surrounding app is built for Apple platforms.

Customize toolbar tool order; number shortcuts follow your configured order. Use Apple Pencil on iPad, including familiar undo and redo gestures. Use mouse and trackpad scroll and zoom gestures on iPad and iPhone. Import PDFs and convert Mermaid diagrams into editable Excalidraw content.

Use Excalidraw collaboration when you want to draw with others.

ExcalidrawZ includes an AI assistant designed for canvas work.

Ask AI to read, create, and revise drawings. Attach images and let AI use visual context when needed. Use proposal previews before applying AI-generated content to the real canvas. Control whether each file is visible to AI. Use AI from compact iPhone toolbars, iPad floating panels, or the macOS inspector.

ExcalidrawZ can expose the current app as an MCP server for compatible AI clients.

Basic mode provides the familiar excalidraw-mcp drawing workflow. Optimized mode adds deeper ExcalidrawZ integration for current-file editing, file navigation, history, canvas inspection, export, library workflows, and math tools. Connect local MCP clients through the app-hosted HTTP endpoint.

ExcalidrawZ includes richer tools for technical drawings and study notes.

Insert LaTeX-rendered formulas. Render function graphs with configurable axes and styles. Use reusable math templates and AI-assisted formula generation. Edit inserted math images later from the canvas.

For sensitive drawings, ExcalidrawZ adds protection around both storage and AI access.

Lock files with local authentication. Encrypt locked files and their checkpoints. Use a Recovery Key for fallback access. Keep locked content hidden from AI; AI can work through proposal canvases instead. Use encrypted backups as an additional recovery path.

ExcalidrawZ supports common export and sharing workflows.

Export images, editable Excalidraw files, and PDF. Preserve editability when exporting .excalidraw.png and .excalidraw.svg. Share through clipboard, files, and the system share sheet. Archive app-managed files for backup.

ExcalidrawZ can open, import, edit, or export common Excalidraw-related formats:

.excalidraw .excalidraw.png .excalidraw.svg PDF import and export image export

Welcome to my Discord server to share suggestions or report issues for ExcalidrawZ.

The Excalidraw core used by ExcalidrawZ is also open-source. You can find it here.

Create Config/Overrides.xcconfig relative to the repository root, alongside Config/Project.xcconfig:

DEVELOPMENT_TEAM = YOUR_TEAM_ID ICLOUD_CONTAINER = iCloud.com.yourname.ExcalidrawZ APP_GROUP_IDENTIFIER = group.com.yourname.ExcalidrawZ

Replace these example values with identifiers registered to your Apple Developer team. The shared configuration leaves DEVELOPMENT_TEAM empty; set your team in the local overrides. The app and QuickLook extension must use the same App Group. All targets, including the extension and tests, inherit the team from Config/Project.xcconfig, which includes your local overrides. These overrides apply to all build configurations.

Create Config/Secrets.plist relative to the repository root. The project already references this file and includes it in both app targets' resources. The app's configuration loader stops with Unable to load Secrets.plist if the file is missing or invalid.

For local drawing development, this minimal configuration is sufficient:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd"> <plist version="1.0"> <dict> <key>COLLAB_URL</key> <string>https://example.com</string> </dict> </plist>

COLLAB_URL must be a valid absolute URL. The example URL is a placeholder for local drawing work; to test collaboration, replace it with the URL of your deployed collaboration-enabled Excalidraw web client.

Optional string keys are ONEDRIVE_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_DRIVE_MACOS_CLIENT_ID, and GOOGLE_DRIVE_IOS_CLIENT_ID. Configure your own OAuth client IDs when developing the corresponding integrations.

Config/Overrides.xcconfig and Config/Secrets.plist are ignored by Git and should stay local.

item.title: Nintendo Takes Down Emulators and Firmware in Massive GitHub DMCA Sweep
item.description:
Nintendo has sent four DMCA takedown notices to GitHub targeting two Nintendo Switch emulators, Yuzu and Citron Neo, along with mod chip firmware.

This isn't the first time Nintendo has sent takedown notices to GitHub, and it's not even the first time it's tried to take down Yuzu, but the focus this time around seems to be on firmware for mod chips. This particular firmware had 144 repositories, all of which have been removed by GitHub and replaced by a DMCA takedown notice. Mod chips like Picofly can be soldered onto the Nintendo Switch's mainboard, and can be flashed with this firmware to circumvent Nintendo's copy protection.

GitHub has posted Nintendo's November 6 DMCA notice, which says, "The Nintendo Switch console and video games contain technological protection measures ('TPMs') that permit the Nintendo Switch console to interact only with legitimate Nintendo video game files. This process protects Nintendo’s copyright-protected video games, (...) by preventing users from playing pirated copies of Nintendo’s video games on the Nintendo Switch console and by preventing users from unlawfully copying and playing Nintendo’s video games on unauthorized devices."

However, while this takedown has effectively wiped out a ton of repositories with mod chip firmware, it seems like it's still being hosted elsewhere on the site, according to TorrentFreak. It's possible, though, that Nintendo isn't finished yet; back in 2024, Nintendo effectively took down 8,500 copies of Yuzu by issuing a takedown that targeted 12 different mirrors of the emulator.

This particular takedown also comes a few days after emulators were able to run the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on PC, so this could be a sign that Nintendo is winding up its lawyers to crack down on emulation once again.

If anything, emulation is a completely different beast in 2026 than it was even in 2024, thanks to the rise of AI. There's already been a wave of AI-made mashup mods that took over Twitter for a couple of weeks, and led Anthropic to coding in a lock to prevent Claude from outright copying games. Game developers have started cracking down on AI ports of games, too. Just last month Rockstar had to take down a browser version of GTA 5, and Bethesda took down an AI-generated Fallout New York game.

item.title: AWS Lambda Web Functions keep billing memory ~7 minutes after the last request
item.description:
Why we chose our own compute over AWS Lambda Web Functions

Lambda Web Functions kept billing memory for 5–7 minutes after the last request, so we built our own compute. On the same Next.js app, it answered warm requests 1.5–3× faster and cold-started about 3.5× faster.

When AWS announced Lambda Web Functions in October, I was excited.

At Easel, we'd spent months building infrastructure to run web applications efficiently on traditional Lambda. Native HTTP servers, concurrent requests, and active CPU billing sounded like exactly what we'd been looking for.

If Web Functions worked the way we hoped, we could potentially replace a substantial amount of our custom infrastructure.

So we decided to put them to the test.

A few weeks later, we'd decided to run our own compute instead. And as it turns out, our own infrastructure was faster, too.

The five-minute problem

Our initial experiments were promising. Web Functions handled 300 concurrent requests without errors, and a new function was serving requests in under nine seconds.

But we quickly ran into something that didn't work for us.

AWS documents that Web Functions bill for memory throughout an execution environment's lifetime, even when no requests are running. What the documentation doesn't specify is how long an idle environment will remain alive before being terminated.

In our tests, environments continued running and accruing memory charges for 5–7 minutes after their last request.

Across six representative environments, we measured idle periods of 313–411 seconds. There was no configurable idle timeout to shorten them.

For a 200ms request followed by 345 seconds of inactivity, that's roughly 1,700 times the request duration in metered memory time.

We checked the economics against CloudWatch and AWS Cost Explorer. Across our experiment, memory accounted for approximately 88% of the calculated compute and request costs at published list prices, even though our application only used around 160–210 MB.

The entire experiment amounted to about two cents at list prices. Hardly alarming on its own.

For an application receiving steady traffic, this may not matter much. The same environment can serve many requests, spreading the idle-memory cost across them.

But Easel needs to support thousands of applications with unpredictable traffic, including many that receive only a handful of requests per day. For those workloads, an environment might spend five minutes waiting for traffic after serving a request that took only a few milliseconds.

Multiply that across thousands of independent deployments, and the economics start to look very different.

We even tried terminating environments ourselves after 10 seconds of inactivity. That reduced metered environment time by roughly 20×, but AWS recorded every intentional exit as a runtime failure.

It wasn't something we wanted to rely on in production.

What if we ran the compute ourselves?

Rather than adopt Web Functions, we decided to move application execution onto servers we operate ourselves, keeping traditional Lambda available for overflow.

This gives us control over scheduling and resource allocation. We can share capacity across applications without paying AWS for each idle environment, and scale beyond our own infrastructure when demand requires it.

Our first self-operated compute host went live in US East on November 2, serving applications including Easel's own website.

But taking ownership of the compute raised another question: How would our performance compare to AWS?

We deployed the same Next.js 16 application to both platforms and ran a series of benchmarks from a client in Ashburn, Virginia.

The results surprised us.

Our host delivered 1.5–3× faster median warm-request times across all four workloads.

The difference wasn't limited to network or routing overhead. Running the same 20,000 chained SHA-256 operations took 29.2ms on our host versus 43.8ms on Web Functions, about 1.5× faster.

And cold starts told a similar story.

After leaving both applications idle for 12 minutes, we triggered fresh execution environments on each platform.

In both trials, Easel started serving requests about 3.5× faster.

We also saw an interesting difference after a shorter idle period. Following one five-minute gap, Web Functions had already terminated its environment and needed 908ms to respond. Easel resumed its paused environment and responded in just 14ms.

These are early results from a single region and a small application, not a comprehensive performance study. The cold-start comparison has only two paired samples, and we haven't benchmarked sustained throughput yet.

Still, seeing our own infrastructure outperform AWS across these initial workloads was encouraging.

Taking ownership of the infrastructure

Running our own compute comes with additional responsibilities. We have to manage capacity, handle failures, and make sure resources are distributed efficiently across applications.

But it also gives us the freedom to optimize the entire execution path, rather than working around the constraints of another platform.

Web Functions may be a good fit for applications with sustained traffic, where idle memory costs are less significant. For Easel, the economics of running large numbers of independent applications led us in a different direction.

And our initial benchmarks suggest that the decision doesn't have to come at the expense of performance.

We're taking on more infrastructure complexity so developers using Easel don't have to.

How we measured Dates Benchmarks ran November 11–12, 2026 (UTC). Idle-memory measurements are from October 26, 2026. Setup The same Next.js 16 application on Easel's self-operated US East host and on AWS Lambda Web Functions in us-east-1. Client One client in Ashburn, Virginia. Timing Time to first byte, excluding TLS connection setup but including network transit and platform routing. Samples About 100 requests per route per platform for warm requests. Two paired trials for cold starts. Hardware The platforms ran on different hardware and resource configurations, so these compare deployments, not normalized hardware. Pricing AWS costs use published list prices.

item.title: Paths in Pieces
item.description:
Paths in pieces

Nov 12th, 2026

Many[1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9] Linux distributions and package managers audit just-built binaries for non-relocatable absolute paths. If a binary contains a path /path/from/build/machine, it might not run on the end-user's machine.

Now, a basic grep on the binary, or a slightly more sophisticated

$ strings bin/app | grep /path/from/build/machine

using GNU binutils's strings will detect these paths, right?

The answer is no, at least when using GCC and targeting x86-64: you should not assume that string constants end up literally in the binary.

Basic example

In this C++ source we create a std::string from a string constant:

#include <iostream> #include <string> #define PREFIX "/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew" int main() { std::string prefix{PREFIX}; std::cout << prefix << '\n'; }

Compile with GCC 12 or later and run, which prints the path:

$ g++ -O2 main.cpp -o main $ ./main /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew

But the path occurs precisely 0 times in the binary itself:

$ grep -acF /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew main 0 $ strings ./main | grep -cF /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew 0

Surely these bytes must be part of the binary somewhere? Let's run strings on it and grep just for the /home prefix:

$ strings ./main | grep /home /home/linuxbrew/xbrew/.linuxbrew

Wait, did GCC just turn

/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew

into an entirely different path

/home/linuxbrew/xbrew/.linuxbrew

with a made-up subdirectory xbrew? How?

Store by pieces

The answer is that GCC optimizes our std::string{PREFIX}. The fact that we see something that looks like the prefix is merely a coincidence.

GCC splits our string up into two (overlapping) pieces of 16 bytes, like so

/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew |--------------|.......... - constant 1 ..........|--------------| - constant 2

which fit exactly in xmm registers, so that it can copy our string to the std::string buffer using vectorized move instructions.

Filtering the relevant bits from g++ -O2 -S -masm=intel, we get

movdqa xmm0, XMMWORD PTR .LC0[rip] movups XMMWORD PTR [rax], xmm0 movdqa xmm0, XMMWORD PTR .LC1[rip] movups XMMWORD PTR 10[rax], xmm0

and our string is stored at .LC0 and .LC1 as constants, which just happen to be next to each other in the binary:

.LC0: .quad 7596498784141404207 .quad 3420313983963919726 .LC1: .quad 7795220194874516088 .quad 8603408430414524009

In general, this happens when a string constant is copied into a buffer, as with std::string, strcpy or memcpy; strings that are only passed around as pointers, like in fopen(PREFIX "/x", "r"), stay intact.

Deduplication

Some package managers like Conda and Spack install packages into a padded prefix during their builds, with the idea that they can be “relocated” to a shorter prefix of the user's choice: the binaries are patched in-place. Conda uses a repeated string _placehold in a directory name to make the prefix long enough.

Now, even if we pick a 256-byte path (a convenient multiple of all x86-64 register widths) by padding the path Conda-style

#define PREFIX "/home/conda/feedstock_root/build_artifacts/" \ "foo_1699999999999/_h_env" \ "_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold" \ "_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold" \ "_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold" \ "_placehold_placehold_placehold_placeho/"

and keep our fingers crossed that GCC puts the pieces of the path contiguously in the binary, we do not see our prefix back in the binary. What we get instead is a much shorter string of only 176 bytes (that is 11 times 16):

$ strings main | grep /home /home/conda/feedstock_root/build_artifacts/foo_1699999999999/_h_env_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placeho/

This is thanks to a further optimization: since the string _placehold repeats every 10 bytes, the 16-byte pieces repeat every lcm(10, 16) = 80 bytes, and GCC needs to store only 5 distinct 16-byte constants for the padding:

/home/conda/feed stock_root/build _artifacts/foo_1 699999999999/_h_ env_placehold_pl acehold_placehol # note d_placehold_plac # that ehold_placehold_ # this placehold_placeh # is old_placehold_pl # cyclic acehold_placeho/ Is this optimization helpful?

For string literals, I don't think so. Clang does not split strings into constants, yet it generates essentially the same instructions. For example, take a longer path, and target AVX2 with -march=x86-64-v3:

#define PREFIX "/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/Cellar/foo/1.2.3/share/foo"

Clang simply puts the string in a section dedicated to strings, .rodata.str1.1:

.L.str: .asciz "/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/Cellar/foo/1.2.3/share/foo"

and copies its 53 bytes with two overlapping 32-byte ymm loads and stores, at offsets 21 and 0:

vmovups ymm0, ymmword ptr [rip + .L.str+21] vmovups ymmword ptr [rax + 21], ymm0 vmovups ymm0, ymmword ptr [rip + .L.str] vmovups ymmword ptr [rax], ymm0

That isn't particularly different from GCC's version, which loads the same two pieces from constants in .rodata.cst32 instead:

vmovdqa ymm0, YMMWORD PTR .LC0[rip] vmovdqu YMMWORD PTR [rax], ymm0 vmovdqa ymm0, YMMWORD PTR .LC1[rip] vmovdqu YMMWORD PTR 21[rax], ymm0

So what does GCC gain? In terms of performance, probably nothing measurable: both do the same loads and stores. With repeated pieces, GCC might have a slight edge, because a repeated piece is loaded once and stored multiple times (11 loads for 16 stores in the earlier example). It also uses aligned reads, but that matters only for ancient CPUs.

In terms of size, GCC's pieces can take more space than the string itself: overlapping bytes are stored twice, and the pieces are aligned to 16, 32 or 64 bytes. The 53-byte path above takes 64 bytes as two pieces, against 54 bytes as a string. It only pays off if it results in deduplication, for example when many strings share a prefix of at least 16 bytes for SSE2, 32 bytes for AVX2, and 64 bytes for AVX-512. Presumably deduplication does not save much in practice, especially now that some distributions use AVX2 as their baseline.

Can I disable this optimization?

Other than compiling with -Os, not really. From GCC 10 onwards (maybe older versions too?) the split-into-pieces optimization triggers for strings up to 256 bytes even without specifying -march. From GCC 12 it is relative to the target's vector width, so longer strings get split too: up to 512 bytes for AVX2 and 1024 bytes for AVX-512.

I believe the only control you have over this is setting the maximum vector width to 128 bits (forcing xmm operations), by passing -mstore-max=128. But this merely restores old defaults, and means strings of up to 256 bytes are still stored in pieces.

Maybe post-hoc scanning is bad practice?

These post-build audits for absolute paths are popular, but you could argue that they are too brittle to start with, so why expect them to work at all?

Indeed, Debian goes much further than a bad-path scan. Their audit asserts that a package can be rebuilt bit for bit in different circumstances: on a different machine, with a different user, time and date, hostname, locale, etc. That is a much more reliable way to keep machine-specific details out of binaries.[10]

I would argue that, despite that, it is still useful to keep string constants literally in the binary, even on Debian, because it improves interpretability of binaries. Running strings ./binary is such a simple and convenient way to get insight into an opaque binary blob, that it outweighs the marginal savings that come with splitting and deduplication. It is reminiscent of Fedora and Ubuntu turning frame pointers back on by default, despite the small overhead, just to make profilers and tracing tools work more reliably.

Other than that, there is the argument of binary patching, which — despite being considered somewhat brittle — is common practice in Conda and Spack: upon install to a user-specified location, the absolute paths are patched in-place accordingly, through what can be seen as a glorified sed invocation. This only works if the path is stored in one piece.

If you'd like to discuss this, a good place is the gcc-patches thread that I started recently, with an initial attempt at a patch that adds a way to opt out.

[1] RPM (Fedora, RHEL, openSUSE): check-buildroot greps every installed file for the build root.

[2] Arch Linux: makepkg warns about references to $srcdir and $pkgdir.

[3] Yocto / OpenEmbedded: the buildpaths QA check.

[4] FreeBSD ports: the stage QA greps for the staging directory.

[5] pkgsrc: CHECK_WRKREF, off unless a package developer turns it on.

[6] Homebrew: brew bottle scans for the prefix to decide whether a bottle is relocatable.

[7] conda-build: files containing the build prefix are listed in info/has_prefix, to be rewritten on install.

[8] rattler-build: the same scheme as conda-build, with memmem.

[9] Julia's BinaryBuilder: check_absolute_paths warns about the build prefix in any file.

[10] Even Debian keeps one path fixed: since early 2024 both builds use the same build directory, because it is recorded in the .buildinfo file and reused when rebuilding. So a build path embedded in a binary goes unnoticed there too.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen
item.description:
Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows.

While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, the Gemini app, Google Search, and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity.

Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

Scaling developer and enterprise workflows

Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows:

Iterative repository coding and debugging: Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash. Open-ended agentic execution: On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on Agent Arena, arena.ai’s live benchmark. For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), ties for #1 on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and leads its class on AutomationBench-AA. Multimodal knowledge work: Hydrogen pairs native 1 million-token input with up to 1 million output tokens to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and recorded video into polished, cited reports and structured deliverables. It outperforms other models on the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows. Web development: On tasks where speed matters to developers, like live UI prototyping, design-to-code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional, feature-complete layouts in fewer prompts. Adaptable speed and intelligence across four thinking levels

We built Gemini 4 Hydrogen for real-world usability. Hydrogen’s four thinking levels — low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier — offer a wide range of options across quality, latency, and cost, scaling in a smooth, predictable progression so you only wait and pay for the reasoning depth a task requires. Across thinking levels, Hydrogen matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class while often finishing tasks faster and using fewer output tokens.

Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search

For consumers, Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes it easier to get things done, staying on track and following instructions more closely across multi-turn conversations.

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen makes your everyday assistant even more helpful — it’s better at following your guidance, calling the right tools, and getting you to a reliable output with less back-and-forth.

Ready-to-go writing, research, and everyday work: Hydrogen sticks closely to your tone, format, and specific rules, so email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try. When you are comparing products or synthesizing dense material, it pulls together clear tables and visual breakdowns without dropping key details. Connects the dots and gets more tasks done: Hydrogen breaks down your goal step-by-step, pulling relevant context from your uploads, Google apps like Gmail and Google Drive, and Connected Apps like Airtable and Dropbox. When you start a task in Gemini, it also more frequently calls the right tools and skills for the job, helping save you time as you check things off your to-do list. Everyday prototyping and iteration: For exploring and testing ideas, Hydrogen generates clean, working layouts in fewer prompts, making it easy to prototype and refine interactive projects quickly, like synthesizing real-time global lightning strike data into an interactive 3D globe.

Hydrogen is significantly upgrading Search, delivering more helpful, intuitive responses for all users globally.

Better understands your true intent: With Hydrogen, you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for. More visual responses: You’ll get highly adaptive, visual, and easy-to-scan responses that are uniquely relevant to your needs, at the speed you expect from Search. Wider range of relevant links: With Hydrogen’s advanced reasoning, we’re also upgrading our query fan-out technique in Search, connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before, helping you find sites you previously might not have discovered. Designed for safe, dependable execution at scale

Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings improvements from our latest Gemini 4 safety and security stack to our broadest audience yet, combining built-in training with real-time surface safeguards to help mitigate both misalignment and misuse. Beyond foundational protections, we focused on two areas that matter most for a faster model that’s for everyday work:

Safe, aligned, and secure agentic workflows: While 3.8 Flash has strong alignment and safeguards, Hydrogen is a leap ahead. It reduces overreach in agentic tasks by up to 81% and under-service by up to 79%, and cuts misaligned actions and task shortcutting across tool-use and coding evaluations by 12x. When faced with impossible or blocked tasks, it is up to 2x less likely to bypass permission boundaries and achieves a 96.7% honesty rate on our internal agent honesty evaluation.Building on our commitment to reasoning transparency, Hydrogen also preserves 99.9% chain-of-thought legibility with zero deceptive reasoning edits across more than 200,000 audited turns. Against indirect prompt injection attacks, Hydrogen is more than 2.3x more resilient on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark, while significantly improving robustness across tool use, computer use, and coding agents. Helpful, reliable everyday interactions: Across our product surfaces, we tuned Hydrogen to make everyday conversations more reliable and safe. Our updated safeguards are also much more precise at distinguishing between real biosecurity risks and legitimate medical or scientific questions — keeping false refusals on HealthBench Pro under 0.4%.

For more details see the Gemini 4 Hydrogen model card.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen, available to everyone today

Starting today, Hydrogen is rolling out globally across our developer, enterprise, and consumer surfaces:

For developers: Build with the Gemini API in AI Studio and the paid tier in Android Studio, try it in AI Studio and if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity. For enterprises: Deploy it in Gemini for business via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, and in Gemini in Google Sheets for eligible business subscriptions. For everyone: Start using it in the Gemini app model drop down 1 and in Google Search for all users, and in Gemini in Google Sheets starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.
